To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
digital angiographic impulse response modeling can be used to estimate the coronary flow and distribution volume of the microcirculation in the normal and diseased heart.

the mean transit time of the microcirculation compartment is linearly related to the flow reserve of the coronary microcirculation, that the mean transit times of both the microcirculation and the arterial compartments are nonlinearly related to the resting coronary flow, that the mean flow/distribution volume of the arterial compartment is linearly correlated with the mean coronary flow, and that the mean transit of the microcirculatory compartment is linearly dependent on the mean flow reserve.
we have developed a mathematical model to quantify coronary flow reserve and microcirculation compartment volume in vivo.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development and validation of a mathematical model that can quantitatively describe the flow and distribution of contrast media through a coronary artery and its associated microcirculation during rest and hyperemic flow states.

developing a method for quantifying the regional myocardial perfusional response to pharmacologic intervention by measuring the transit time of radiographic contrast media through the epicardial and microcirculatory coronary vessels.
the application of a mathematical model to describe and quantitate the regional distribution of blood flow in a canine model with selective digital angiography.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the impulse response analysis technique is a useful method for quantitating regional coronary flow, coronary flow reserve, and myocardial microcirculatory distribution volumes.
the model compartments are functionally descriptive of their anatomic counterparts, but that the model compartments cannot be directly related to anatomic structures.
this technique provides a method for the quantitative analysis of regional myocardium perfusion and the estimation of coronary flow reserve and microcirculatory distribution volume.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the model impulse response function can be used to quantify regional coronary flow, flow reserves, and distribution volume in normal and stenosed vessels in the canine left anterior descending coronary artery system.
the model impulse response analysis is a powerful tool for quantifying coronary flow and distribution volume in the intact animal.
the model compartments are a useful tool for the quantification of coronary hemodynamics and microvascular autoregulation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to use a single angiographic impulse response measurement to estimate coronary flow and flow reserve, and that this method may be applicable in humans.
we have developed a method to quantify coronary flow and distribution volume in the microvasculature from digital angiographic impulse response functions.
the compartmental transit time analysis of coronary flow reserve is a useful method to quantitatively assess microvascular function in vivo.
